title: Intermediate‐Scale Testing of Multiphase Processes in Subsurface Contamination: Opportunities for Carbon Storage and Land–Atmosphere Exchange
content:
Abstract

Understanding multiphase flow and transport in porous media is essential for addressing a wide range of subsurface hydrological, environmental, and earth systems problems. Multiphase processes can involve the movement, trapping, and dissolution of fluid phases within soil pores. Geological heterogeneity across scales—from pore to field—further complicates their behavior. Quantifying subsurface multiphase processes in the field remains a significant challenge. Such data sets are often limited to sparse borehole and well observations; analyses therefore carry considerable uncertainty because initial conditions are poorly defined, natural boundary conditions cannot be controlled, and geological characterization is incomplete at relevant scales. Models validated under these constraints are often site-specific and not broadly generalizable across diverse geological and climate settings. Intermediate-scale laboratory testing (IST) complements traditional column and field experimentation by improving fundamental process understanding, refining conceptual models, and supporting model/theory validation under conditions that are impractical or impossible to obtain in the field. IST uses synthetic aquifers with designed heterogeneity that capture key features, allowing researchers to replicate and measure field processes at high spatiotemporal resolution under well-defined initial conditions and carefully controlled boundary conditions. This paper reviews key advancements in IST, highlighting examples from decades of research on subsurface contamination by nonaqueous-phase chemicals. It also discusses and envisions how this approach can address current and emerging problems related to carbon storage, greenhouse gas management, and soil-plant-atmosphere systems.
